title: Cartwright — WebMCP-native storefronts
pitch: An open-source engine that scaffolds complete webshops where every page ships typed WebMCP tools — shown on a real coffee shop, with a test-enforced line: the purchase stays the human's.
about_excerpt: An open-source engine that scaffolds complete webshops where every page ships typed WebMCP tools — shown on a real coffee shop, with a test-enforced line: the purchase stays the human's. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What it is, and why WebMCP (the use case) In-browser AI agents act on websites by guessing at the DOM — brittle selectors, scraping, silent failures, no way to verify what happened. WebMCP fixes that at the platform level: the page declares tools, the agent calls them. But it only matters if sites actually implement it, and hand-wiring agent tools for every page of every site does not scale. Cartwright is an open-source (MIT) engine that scaffolds complete stores — design system, database, cart, checkout, admin, i18n — with one command. During the challenge window we made the engine WebMCP-native : webshop templates now scaffold with the surface ON ( npx create-cartwright my-shop --template coffee → a store whose every page registers typed, page-contextual tools via document.modelContext the moment an agent-capable browser opens it). Not one agent-ready site — a generator of them. Shopify has shown storefront-scale WebMCP for its hosted platform; this is the same idea for the self-hosted, open-source world: the whole engine is MIT, and every scaffold owns its stack. WebMCP leverage — the depth of the surface 13 tools on the demo shop, three registration styles, one shared core: Site-wide (imperative): search_products (reduced, bounded rows — no checkout endpoints or internal fields ever enter the browser surface), get_cart (verification-rich returns: line handles, stock ceilings, structured money), same-origin navigate . Contextual, per route — progressive disclosure (the shape proposed in the tool-collections discussion, webmcp#255): an agent only ever sees the collection that makes sense on the page it is on. The product page registers add_current_product_to_cart with the page's live variants as natural-language enum values ("Whole beans, 250 g" — not internal ids), prices and stock in the descriptor. The cart page registers update_cart_item_quantity / remove_cart_item (line ids enumerated in the schema) / go_to_checkout . The catalogue page registers list_visible_products (exactly what the human sees, zero network) and filter_products (schema server-derived from the live categories). Declarative forms: search, contact and newsletter carry toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription attributes — the form itself is the tool, answered via SubmitEvent.respondWith (preventDefault-first). toolautosubmit only on read-only search; the human confirms communication. Agent activity is visible : :tool-form-active styling highlights the form the agent is filling. Design-pack tools: the homepage brew calculator is also calculate_brew_ratio — the same math module serves the human's widget and the agent's tool, so the two can never disagree. Any design pack can ship tools ( DesignPack.webMcpToolBindings ); the safety tests aggregate them all. The engine also answers the frameworks meta-issue (webmcp#199) in shipped, test-pinned code: execute() reads state freshly at execution time (never captured props); effect dependencies are serialized props, so re-renders never thrash the registry; every mount owns an AbortSignal and cleanup runs before the next route's registrations (abort-then-register, the current-spec-safe order — our e2e fake rejects duplicate names, and a soft-navigation spec proves the swap inside one document); one rejecting registration cannot drop the tools after it. One governed tool registry, two transports: the same operations back the in-page WebMCP tools for browsing agents and a server-side MCP endpoint ( /api/mcp ) for headless agents — same session, same state in the browser; same scopes and audit trail on the server. Beneath the callable layer sits the readable and discoverable one: llms.txt with capability truth, JSON-LD on every citable page, content negotiation (the homepage serves markdown to agents that ask), an ARD catalog, OpenAPI — and on the payable side the engine carries protocol-pluralistic commerce rails (ACP endpoints and UCP identity-linking on the same engine), so the merchant doesn't have to bet. Readable, discoverable, callable, payable — one engine. Execution — a complete product, tested like one This is a production Next.js 16 App Router application deployed on Vercel: a real store with a live database, working cart and checkout, an admin, and i18n — not a mock. The WebMCP layer is held to the same bar: ~100 unit tests across the registrar, the per-route mounts, the declarative forms, the pack tool, and the safety moat (below). A Playwright e2e suite installs a faithful fake document.modelContext (current spec semantics: duplicate-name rejection, pre-aborted-signal rejection) and walks home → catalogue → product → cart → checkout, including one real add-to-cart round-trip against the database and a soft-navigation leg that proves route teardown inside one document. Evaluation-driven, with the Chrome team's own harness: we ran GoogleChromeLabs/webmcp-tools' webmcp-evals (smoke mode) against the live demo — 12/12 steps green across brew-ratio, cart reads, catalogue listing/filtering, search, a real add-to-cart and the checkout handoff (runner webmcp-evals@0.0.3 , repo commit d39eae4 , 2026-08-27). The run's three genuine findings (a prefetch loop on the empty-cart page, non-canonical URLs in two tool returns, Danish parameter names on an English store) were fixed the same day — the eval harness caught real bugs, which is the point of running it. Byte-identity discipline: with the flag off, no registrar mounts, no tool* attribute renders, the HTML is byte-identical — pinned by tests. The live surface is smoke-monitored : the store's deployment gate asserts /en/webmcp-check and the pack tool on every run. Potential impact — who this is for Every small store that will never hand-write agent tools. The economics only work at the engine level: implement WebMCP once, correctly, with tests — and every scaffolded site inherits it. The demo is a real storefront a judge can buy from (demo checkout), running the exact code a scaffold produces. And the scaffold proves it in a first minute: npx create-cartwright myshop --template coffee && cd myshop && npm run dev seeds the demo's own nine-product catalogue — images, stock, attributes, and real variants on one product (an agent must handle both shapes) — so the tools have something true to act on with no config and no API keys. The same engine runs a second live vertical (eyewear, different design pack, Danish locale) — the surface is engine-level, not bespoke to one demo. Creativity & ambition — the line we drew The collaboration model is explicit: the agent gets the errands, the human keeps the decisions. Every cart mutation returns the fresh cart, so the agent verifies instead of assumes; an ambiguous mid-request failure says so and routes the agent through get_cart before any retry
video_transcript_excerpt: This is Cartright, running live inside chat GPT's built-in browser. Every new web shop it creates includes web MCP from the first run. The page gives the agent type tools, not pixels to scrape. The cart starts empty. The shop's own search tool finds a bright single origin coffee. On its product page, a web MCP tool adds exactly two bags and returns the fresh cart state. At checkout, the agent stops. No personal details are invented and no order tool is exposed. The errand is automated. The final decision stays human. The same storefront can answer a brewing question instantly. To brew three bright cups, use 35 g of coffee and 600 g of water at a 1:17 ratio. This is the multiplier. It is not one web MCP demo store. It is a generator for web MCP native commerce. Run the single command shown on screen. One command creates an open source storefront with page contextual tools already included and switched on.

live_observation.first_impression: A polished Northbound Coffee Roasters storefront presents product categories, search, cart, currency/language controls, and a coffee-dose calculator. The purpose as a coffee shop is immediately clear, with WebMCP/API links visible in the footer.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked the featured Northbound Espresso Blend product link and then the cart link.
live_observation.after_state: The page remained on the storefront and the cart still showed 0 items; no product detail or cart transition was observed.
live_observation.notes: Storefront content and agent-oriented links are visible, but the attempted product interaction did not visibly navigate or add anything.
